Done. `python3 -m pytest -q` → **11 passed**.

The implementation in `money/money.py:9` is short, but the ordering in it is doing the real work — round, *then* read the sign, *then* render:

- **`str()` before `Decimal`** is the non-obvious one. `Decimal(0.995)` is `0.99499999…` — the nearest binary double sits *below* the decimal midpoint — so rounding it half-up gives `$0.99` and fails `test_rounding_boundaries`. Round-tripping through `str()` rounds `"0.995"`, the value the caller actually wrote. Note that `0.005` lands just *above* its midpoint and would have passed either way, so that test alone wouldn't have caught this; `0.995` is what forces it.
- **Sign is read after rounding**, so `-0.004` → `$0.00` rather than `($0.00)`.
- **The zero test is `value < 0`, not a sign-bit check.** `-0.004` quantizes to `Decimal("-0.00")` and `-0.0` reprs as `"-0.0"`; both are *signed*, so `is_signed()` would call them negative. A value comparison is false for every flavour of zero.
- **Grouping is applied to the rounded value**, so `999.999` → `$1,000.00` keeps the carry into the new separator.

Beyond the suite I spot-checked carry-into-grouping, `0.1 + 0.2`, a non-ASCII currency symbol, `1e9`, and `group=False` on a negative — all correct. `SOLUTION.md` records the approach and why each of these edge cases constrains it. I left `tests/` untouched and made no commits.
